transcript:
Live from NPR News, I'm Lakshmi Singh.
One of Krista Pike's lawyers says she is alive and hospitalized in critical condition
a day after the state of Tennessee tried to execute her by lethal injection for 1995 murder.
Stephen Farrell with Federal Defender Services of Eastern Tennessee says this outcome is
exactly what Pike feared would happen.
We presented evidence that due to her blood condition, venous access would be difficult,
and that this type of prolonged execution that she didn't want to happen would happen.
Tennessee officials are now trying to determine how Pike survived two doses of pentobarbital,
a lethal drug used in multiple states that carry out the death penalty.
Tennessee Governor Bill Lee has halted further executions in his state pending a third-party
review.
President Trump promised that he would campaign to support Republicans in 35 of the most competitive
races, but NPR's Frank Ordonez reports he is kicking off a campaign swing in the more
comfortably red states of Oklahoma and Texas, while Vice President Vance is in Florida.
Starting in Oklahoma is a chance to knock off some rust and workshop his campaign speech
in front of a more friendly environment, but it reminds Alex Conan, who worked in the George
W. Bush White House of the 2006 midterms, when Bush campaigned almost exclusively in
red states.
You can't go to a district or a state where there's just as many Democrats as Republicans
or where there's a lot of independent voters because you're going to do more harm than
good when your favorability numbers are this low.
That's because in a swing state, Trump is likely and perhaps more likely to stir up Democrats
and independent voters to go out and vote against Republicans, Franco, Ordonez, NPR News.
And here's Vance in Lakeland, Florida today.
If anybody was unsure, I would say by the turnout today, it seems very obvious that
Florida is MAGA country and it's great to be in Central Florida.
In other news, President Trump has announced that South Korea will invest $200 billion
in energy projects.
That's part of a $350 billion investment deal that South Korea agreed to last year.
More from NPR's Anthony Kuhn.
The projects include a gas-fired power plant in Texas, eight large nuclear power plants
in several states, and investment in a natural gas pipeline in Alaska.
President Trump called the projects a major step towards securing the U.S.'s energy supply
chain.
The announcement's timing is widely seen as a bid to burnish Trump's economic record ahead
of midterm elections.
South Korea's Ministry of Industry, though, says in a statement that there's been no
decision on whether or how much South Korea will invest in the Alaska pipeline.
A U.S. Commerce Department fact sheet says that whether work on the project goes ahead
depends on whether it's considered commercially viable.
Anthony Kuhn, NPR News, Seoul.
From Washington, this is NPR News.
New York is leading a coalition of 21 states as well as Washington, D.C., New York City,
Chicago, and Denver, ensuing to stop the Trump administration from repealing a rule that
limits emissions from power plants.
The lawsuit argues the administration's actions will give the nation's biggest polluters
a free pass that will set the U.S. back decades in its fight against climate change.
In his speech to the United Nations last year, President Trump called climate change the
greatest con job ever perpetrated on the world.
California Governor Gavin Newsom has signed into state law a bill prohibiting hospitals
from using artificial intelligence to replace the clinical judgment of health care professionals,
and Piers Andrea Shue reports the legislation was sponsored by a union representing 100,000
nurses statewide.
The California Nurses Association says the new law gives patients and health care workers
landmark protections against unsafe use of AI.
Among other things, it prohibits unlicensed staff from using AI to perform tasks that
can only be done by licensed professionals.
The governor's office says the protections keep people, not algorithms, at the center
of health care decisions.
But Newsom vetoed a second bill that would have explicitly protected health care workers
from retaliation for overriding AI-generated recommendations.
The governor took issue with how such cases would be adjudicated, noting the California
Labor Commission lacks the specialized medical expertise needed to resolve such disputes.
Andrea Shue, NPR News.
This is NPR.
Stay tuned for the following announcements and messages from our sponsors.

topics.text: Krista Pike survives execution attempt in Tennessee; governor halts further executions pending review
President Trump campaigns in Oklahoma and Texas while Vice President Vance campaigns in Florida
South Korea announces $200 billion investment in U.S. energy projects including nuclear plants
New York leads coalition of 21 states suing to stop Trump administration from repealing power plant emissions rule
California Governor Newsom signs law prohibiting hospitals from using AI to replace clinical judgment of health care professionals
